To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

pre service teachers' selfreported knowledge of students with disabilities and their perceived competence to teach students with exceptional needs were not significantly related to their age, parental status, or exposure to special education and inclusive education units.

the participants in this study were knowledgeable about students with exceptionalities, perceived themselves as being competent to teach these students in inclusive classrooms, and had a positive attitude towards inclusion.

(a) pre service teachers' self-reported knowledge and perceived competence in teaching students with exceptionalities was low; (b) pre service teachers with more experience in the field of teaching students with exceptional needs had a greater knowledge base; (c) pre service teachers who had completed more courses on special education and/or inclusive education had a greater knowledge of exceptionalities; and (d) pre service teachers were more positive about teaching in an inclusive environment when they had greater knowledge of exceptional needs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the preparation of teachers to teach students with exceptionalities.
the knowledge base of pre service teachers, their perceptions of competence and their general attitude toward teaching students with special needs in an inclusive setting.
the initial teacher preparation for teaching students with exceptionalities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the teacher education students surveyed in this study were not well prepared to teach students with exceptionalities in inclusive settings, and that the university was not providing adequate preparation.
there are no significant differences between pre service teachers' knowledge of, perceived competence, and attitude toward teaching students with exceptional needs.

pre-service teachers' perceptions of knowledge and competence in teaching students with exceptionalities were not influenced by their age, gender, parental status, exposure to units of studies in special or inclusive education, or their general attitude toward teaching students with exceptional needs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of pre service teachers in our sample felt they were competent to teach all students with exceptionality in the inclusive classroom.
the majority of pre-service teachers in the study reported that their knowledge about students in the exceptional categories was low and their perceived competence was low.

teacher educators need to be mindful that the concept of exceptionalities is broad, and that teacher education students need opportunities to learn about the diversity of exceptionalities in order to develop the necessary knowledge and skills to be effective teachers of students with exceptionalities.
The main takeaway from our work is that

pre-service teachers are generally not well equipped to meet the challenges of educating all students in inclusive classrooms, regardless of their age, parental status or exposure to special education.
teacher educators should be aware that pre service teachers are not necessarily aware that they have a responsibility to teach all learners in their classroom, including those with special needs.
teacher education programs need to provide a broader conceptualization of exceptionalities in the classroom and that this is not being adequately addressed.
